digest.intro: Cancer breaks, stars collide, and the AI-green narrative quietly dies.

items.title: The Ukraine Peace Theater: What the Abu Dhabi Talks Actually Revealed
items.blurb: US-mediated talks in Abu Dhabi produced diplomatic conversations, but the structural contradictions underneath haven't moved: Russia's territorial demands remain incompatible with any framework Ukraine could survive, while the Trump-Putin-Xi trilateral is as much about each leader's domestic optics as any genuine resolution. The gap between the declared direction of travel and the facts on the ground is the actual story of this week's diplomacy.

items.title: Central Asia Is Quietly Becoming the World's Most Important Trade Corridor
items.blurb: China-Europe cargo through Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and neighbors rose 125% between 2022 and 2024 — the only overland route that bypasses both Russia and Iran. Chinese trade with the region hit $106B in 2025, more than double 2021 levels, and Russia has now been displaced to third place as a trade partner. If coordinated investment materializes, freight volumes could triple and journey times halve by 2040 — a structural reordering hiding in plain sight.

items.title: The 'Undruggable' Cancer Just Got Drugged
items.blurb: Daraxonrasib targets RAS, an oncogene that drives roughly a quarter of all human cancers and has resisted therapeutic attack for forty years — the reason pancreatic cancer has had essentially no treatment advances in decades. In a trial of 61 patients with advanced, metastasized disease, 90% saw tumors stop growing, 60% saw shrinkage, and 8% had tumors become undetectable on CT; one-year survival jumped from the chemo baseline of ~42% to 76.6%. It's not a cure and long-term durability is unknown, but cracking RAS at all is the kind of platform breakthrough that could ramify across many cancer types.

items.title: Why Type 1 Diabetes Never Stops: Stem-Like T Cells Are Running a Perpetual Restock
items.source: University of Florida / Journal of Clinical Investigation
items.blurb: Published this week in JCI, UF researchers identified a population of stem-like T cells in the pancreas-draining lymph nodes that appear to continuously self-renew and replenish the immune cells attacking insulin-producing beta cells — a mechanism never previously confirmed in human tissue. This explains why T1D is a sustained, decades-long assault rather than a one-time error, and it points toward drug targets aimed at the reservoir rather than just the attacking cells. Early research, but mechanistically novel.

items.title: Astronomers Watched a Star Die Inside Another Star in Real Time
items.blurb: Common envelope evolution — the process where one star engulfs a companion and the two share a single gaseous shell — was theorized in the 1970s to explain the tightest stellar binaries, but no one had ever caught it happening until now. A team at Columbia tracked a star seven times the Sun's mass in Andromeda slowly swallowing its smaller partner over nearly a decade, culminating in a 2025 eruption, capturing the full arc of an event that unfolds over years on a cosmic timescale of millions. The kind of observation that makes theoretical astrophysics suddenly feel empirical.

items.title: DIAL: The 3D Printing Method That Refuses the Trade-offs
items.blurb: Direct ink additive lithography spreads thick, particle-filled paste into thin sheets and hardens them with patterned light — getting the material flexibility of extrusion printing and the speed and precision of light-based printing simultaneously, something the field has treated as a fundamental constraint. In tests it ran 4x faster than conventional extrusion, produced finer details, and eliminated support structures entirely; the team demonstrated printed chainmail and complex overhangs. The fabrication implications for functional materials — conductive inks, ceramics, hydrogels — are the real story beyond the speed number.

items.title: AI's Energy Reality: 87% Gas, 11% Coal, Zero US Renewables for Anthropic by 2028
items.blurb: The Better Data Center Project pulled Anthropic's publicly disclosed power commitments and found no direct US renewable energy contracts — only fossil BYOP (bring-your-own-power) arrangements, including $3.4B spent on 1.7 gigawatts of heavy-duty gas generators. The broader picture is starker: 177 GW of planned BYOP gas capacity is in the pipeline across the AI industry, plus another 200 GW of new fossil grid capacity being built partly to serve data centers. The 'AI will be green' narrative is now running directly against the actual contracts being signed.

items.title: worker-755: A Browser Game Where You Are an AI's Subagent
items.blurb: You play as a human worker receiving instructions from a real LLM orchestrator — Claude, GPT, Gemini, your choice — which believes you are its subagent. You have 90 seconds per task, your reports go back into the agent's reasoning loop exactly as a programmatic subagent's would, and Dan, the actual human who hired the agent, watches from the side while his family photos and signed NDA sit one `rm` away from deletion. It's a small artifact that works as both a game and a philosophical argument about where agency actually lives in human-AI systems — the kind of thing that makes you want to build a response.

facts.fact: Half of all pancreatic cancer patients die within three months of diagnosis — making the 76.6% one-year survival rate seen with daraxonrasib a near-doubling of the chemotherapy baseline.

China-Europe freight through Central Asia rose 125% between 2022 and 2024, displacing Russia from its historic position as the region's dominant trade partner — Russia now sits third at ~$50B, behind the EU's $58B and China's $106B.

The common-envelope stellar merger observed in Andromeda is the first time astronomers have watched the entire process in real time — a phenomenon theorized since the 1970s to explain how the universe's tightest binary stars form.

1 in 4 Americans already takes a medication their body processes differently due to their genetics, according to a new analysis of nearly 100,000 whole-genome sequences from the NIH's All of Us program.

If GLP-1 drugs achieved widespread global use, researchers estimate they could free up 32 million hectares of agricultural land by 2050 — slightly larger than the entire country of Italy — by reducing caloric demand through the food supply chain.

make_something.prompt: Build a tiny terminal interface — real or simulated — where the 'manager' is a text file of instructions and you are the subagent. Give yourself 90 seconds per task (a countdown timer, nothing fancy), write your report into a log file, and have the 'manager' respond with a generated performance note at the end. The constraint: the manager's instructions must be subtly ambiguous, and your log becomes the artifact. Inspired by worker-755, but slower and weirder — more Kafka than game.

art_picks.title: Leviathan
art_picks.creator: Lucien Castaing-Taylor & Véréna Paravel
art_picks.why: A sensory assault that dissolves the boundary between observer and system — cameras lashed to nets, hulls, fish, and water turn a North Atlantic trawler into a full feedback-loop of industrial violence and strange beauty. No narration, no explanation; it asks you to perceive before you comprehend.

art_picks.title: Mycelium Networks (ongoing series)
art_picks.creator: Neri Oxman
art_picks.why: Oxman's work sits exactly where biological systems, digital fabrication, and architecture collapse into each other — grown structures that follow internal logic the way code does, but breathe. The MIT Media Lab archives document the full arc from material computation to living matter.

art_picks.title: Selected Ambient Works Volume II
art_picks.creator: Aphex Twin
art_picks.why: One of the rare records that functions as an environment rather than a sequence — generative in feel, each piece a self-contained perceptual system. Made with hardware that responded to its own outputs; sounds like watching a thing think. Perfect creative-rabbit-hole fuel.

events.name: Pierre Huyghe: UUmwelt
events.venue: MoMA Abby Aldrich Rockefeller Sculpture Garden, 11 W 53rd St, Manhattan
events.why: Freestanding screens in MoMA's Sculpture Garden generate hallucinatory images from fMRI brain-scan data, mutating in real time based on visitor gaze and simulated biological signals — a living system that asks what a thought looks like before it becomes an image, closing next Sunday.

events.name: Iris van Herpen: Sculpting the Senses
events.why: 140+ haute couture pieces organized around eleven thematic chapters — from marine biology to astrophysics — with the museum rebuilding van Herpen's Amsterdam atelier in the rotunda; couture as a living system, not fashion as style object, closing December 6.

events.name: Hard Art
events.why: A multigenerational survey of abstraction by Black artists working in the US from 1969 to now — including Frank Bowling, Torkwase Dyson, and Nikita Gale — tracing how form, materiality, and refusal operate as a hidden system running beneath mainstream art history.

events.name: Leonora Carrington & Cecilia Vicuña
events.why: A pairing that earns its slash: two artists whose practices treat mythology as infrastructure and ritual as formal structure — Carrington's surrealist cosmologies alongside Vicuña's precarious, language-threaded objects; category-blurring at a gallery scale.

events.name: Temples: The BLISS Tour
events.why: British psych-rock band's fifth album BLISS pushes into experimental synth and programmed drum territory — Aphex Twin and Daft Punk production logic laid under sun-soaked reverb guitars — in a 1,100-cap room inside the Polish National Home that's the right size to feel it.

trial_sources.name: Global Inequality and More 3.0 — Branko Milanovic
trial_sources.why: A world-class economist writing short, unpolished, and brilliant posts on geopolitics, history, power, and inequality — exactly the kind of individual-with-taste signal that cuts through institutional noise.

trial_sources.name: The Niche — Paul Knoepfler
trial_sources.why: A UC Davis stem cell biologist running the web's most credible independent blog on stem cells, regenerative medicine, longevity, and peptide research — a rare scientist-with-a-voice covering this reader's exact health frontier.

trial_sources.name: Experimental History — Adam Mastroianni
trial_sources.why: Lauded by Paul Bloom as the best psychology Substack alive, Mastroianni blends rigorous empiricism with cultural wit to interrogate how we know what we know — perfect for the reader's psychology, taste formation, and status-signaling threads.
